docs.title: CLI Shortcuts & Hotkeys
docs.text: YAICLI offers a rich set of keyboard shortcuts and interactive features to enhance your command-line experience. This page covers all available shortcuts and interactive functionalities.

docs.title: Global Shortcuts
docs.text:
These shortcuts work in all interactive modes:

Shortcut Description Ctrl+C Clear the current input line (during generation: cancel the turn); press twice quickly to exit Ctrl+D Exit the application Shift+Tab Toggle between Chat/Execute modes Ctrl+R Search command history ↑/↓ Navigate through command history Ctrl+L Clear the screen Ctrl+A Move cursor to beginning of line Ctrl+E Move cursor to end of line Ctrl+U Clear charactors before cursor Ctrl+W Delete word before cursor

docs.title: History Navigation
docs.text:
When searching history with Ctrl+R:

Shortcut Description Ctrl+R Cycle through matching history items Enter Select current history item Esc Cancel history search

docs.title: Interactive Commands
docs.text:
YAICLI provides special commands that begin with a slash (/) or an exclamation mark (!):

Command Description /help or /? Show help message /clear Clear the current conversation history /his Show chat history /list List all saved chat sessions /save <title> Save the current chat session with a title /load <index> Load a saved chat session /del <index> Delete a saved chat session /exit Exit the application /mode chat\|exec Switch between chat and execute modes !<command> Execute a shell command directly

With !<command>, you can execute a shell command directly without leaving the interactive mode. For example, !ls -al will list files in the current directory, !git status will show the git status, etc.

docs.title: Auto-Suggestion
docs.text:
YAICLI offers auto-suggestions based on your command history. As you type, it shows light gray text suggesting completions from your history:

  • Press → (right arrow) to accept the full suggestion
  • Continue typing to ignore the suggestion
  • Press Esc then f to accept one word of the suggestion

To disable auto-suggestions, set AUTO_SUGGEST=false in your configuration.

docs.title: Multi-line and Long Input
docs.text:
The interactive prompt is deliberately single-line: Enter submits the current line, so Alt+Enter / Esc+Enter also submit rather than insert a newline. For long or multi-line prompts, pass the text as a quoted argument or pipe it:

# Quote a multi-line string
ai "$(cat prompt.txt)"

# Pipe content and add an instruction
cat error.log | ai "Explain these errors"

# Here-document
ai "$(cat <<'EOF'
Summarize the following log and list the root cause:
<paste log here>
EOF
)"

Piped stdin is combined with the prompt argument (stdin content comes first).

docs.title: Command Editing
docs.text:
When in Execute mode and reviewing a suggested command:

Option Description e Edit the command before execution y Execute the command as is n Cancel execution

When editing a command:

  • The full command is presented in an editable field
  • Make your changes and press Enter to execute
  • Press Esc to cancel the edit

docs.title: Visual Indicators
docs.text:
YAICLI uses visual indicators to help you understand the current state:

Indicator Meaning 💬 > Chat mode prompt 🚀 > Execute mode prompt Cursor animation Processing your request Syntax highlighting Code in responses

docs.title: Input Methods
docs.text: YAICLI accepts input through various methods:

docs.title: Direct Input
docs.text: ai "What is the capital of France?"

docs.title: Piped Input
docs.text: echo "What is the capital of France?" | ai

docs.title: File Analysis
docs.text: cat error.log | ai "Explain these errors"

docs.title: Combined Input
docs.text: cat data.csv | ai "Convert this CSV to JSON"

docs.title: Image Input
docs.text:
# Local image file
ai --image photo.jpg "What is in this image?"

# Multiple images
ai -i img1.png -i img2.png "Compare these"

# Image URL
ai --image https://example.com/photo.jpg "Describe this"

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
YAICLI returns a non-zero exit status for failures it can detect, so scripts and CI can tell success from failure:

Exit code Meaning 0 Success (answer produced; informational commands such as --version, --list-*). 1 A handled failure: invalid/malformed configuration, unknown or misconfigured provider, missing/invalid API key or API error, retry exhaustion, no input/aborted action, or an unexpected error printed as Unknown error: .... 2 Usage error: an invalid option or argument. 3 A tool call was denied and --fail-on-tool-denied was set. 130 Interrupted by SIGINT (Ctrl+C) during a one-shot run or generation. 141 Broken pipe (EPIPE); ai --help \| head -1 is safe and exits 0/141.

A failure report such as Unknown error: API_KEY is required is accompanied by exit code 1; if you see a failure message with exit code 0, that is a bug. Verify the current build with:

ai --version; echo "exit=$?"

Inside the interactive --chat REPL, an error during one turn is printed and the session continues; the process exits 0 when you leave the REPL normally. Use single-shot mode (-p or a prompt argument) when you need the exit code to reflect the request outcome. The full scripting contract (JSON output, signals, non-interactive approvals) is in Headless & Scripting.

docs.text:

docs.title: Command Reference
docs.text: YAICLI provides a versatile command-line interface with multiple options and modes. This page covers all available commands and options.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
ai [OPTIONS] [PROMPT]

Where PROMPT is the text input for the agent. If not provided, YAICLI reads from stdin when it is piped; with no prompt and no stdin it starts the interactive REPL. Use -p/--print to force a single one-shot run, and see Headless & Scripting for the full scripting contract.

docs.title: Command Line Reference
docs.text: Here's a comprehensive list of all available options:

docs.title: Core Options
docs.text: Option Short Description --help -h Show help message and exit --verbose -V Show verbose output (loaded config, API calls, etc.) --version -v Show version and exit (fast path; does not read config) --template Show the default config file template and exit --list-providers List available providers and exit

docs.title: Headless / Scripting Options
docs.text:
Option Short Description --print -p Explicit one-shot mode: run once, never start the REPL --output-format text\|json\|stream-json Output format for the result (default text; stream-json is NDJSON events) --quiet -q Only print the answer to stdout (no labels/progress) --max-turns N Maximum tool-call rounds for this run (overrides MAX_TOOL_CALL_DEPTH) --yes -y Auto-approve read-level tools only; write/exec tools still need a rule --allowed-tools "a,b*" Per-run tool allowlist, comma-separated names or globs --cwd DIR Working directory / workspace root for the run --fail-on-tool-denied Exit with code 3 when a tool was denied

See Headless & Scripting for JSON schemas, exit codes and signal handling, and Permissions & Safety for --yes / --allowed-tools semantics.

docs.title: Common Command Examples
docs.text:
# Agent task: let the model pick and run tools
ai "Use your tools to find the 3 largest files here and write a summary to REPORT.md"

# One-shot with machine-readable output
ai -p "summarize the git log" --output-format json

# Answer-only output (for pipelines)
ai -q -p "list the open TODOs in src/"

# Get a quick answer
ai "What is the capital of France?"

# Start an interactive chat session
ai --chat

# Save chat with a title
ai --chat "Python programming tips"

# Generate and execute shell commands
ai --shell "Create a backup of my Documents folder"

# Generate code snippets (Python by default)
ai --code "Write a function to sort a list"

# Use a specific LLM model
ai --model gpt-4-turbo "Explain quantum computing"

# Adjust temperature for more creative responses
ai --temperature 0.8 "Write a poem about AI"

# Create a custom role
ai --create-role "SQL Expert"

# Use a custom role
ai --role "SQL Expert" "Optimize this query"

# Show verbose output for debugging
ai --verbose "Test query"

# Send an image to a vision model
ai --image photo.jpg "What is in this image?"

# Send multiple images for comparison
ai -i img1.png -i img2.png "Compare these screenshots"

# Send an image URL
ai --image https://example.com/photo.jpg "Describe this"

# Image-only (no text prompt)
ai --image diagram.png

docs.title: Interactive Mode Commands
docs.text:
When in interactive chat or shell mode, you can use these special commands:

Command Description /help or /? Show help message /clear Clear conversation history /his Show chat history /list List saved chats /save <title> Save current chat with title /load <index> Load a saved chat /del <index> Delete a saved chat /exit Exit the application /mode chat\|exec Switch between chat and execute modes /add <path> Add file or directory to context /context or /ctx Show estimated context/token usage for the current conversation /context <subcmd> Manage file context (list, add, remove, clear) /compact [keep_rounds] Compact the conversation, keeping the last N turns /permissions List session approvals, the persistent allowlist and the numbered rules /permissions revoke <tool-or-index> Remove a persistent permission by tool name or rule number (the tool will ask again)

docs.title: Context Management Commands
docs.text:
The /add and /context commands help you manage files and directories in the conversation context:

Command Description /add <path> Add a file or directory to the persistent context /context list or /ctx list List all items in current context /context clear or /ctx clear Remove all items from context /context add <path> Add item to context (same as /add) /context remove <path> or /ctx remove <path> Remove specific item from context

Context Features:

  • Persistent: Items added with /add stay in context for the entire session
  • Smart reading: Files are read and formatted for AI consumption
  • Directory support: Directories are scanned recursively (2 levels deep by default)
  • Auto-ignores: Skips .git, node_modules, __pycache__, .venv, etc.
  • Flexible matching: Use partial paths or filenames for removal

Example:

💬 > /add src/main.py
Added file to context: /path/to/src/main.py

💬 > /add tests/
Added directory to context: /path/to/tests/

💬 > /context list
┏━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Type   ┃ Path                          ┃
┡━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ FILE   │ src/main.py                   │
│ DIR    │ tests/                        │
└────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

💬 > /context remove main.py

💬 > /ctx clear
Context cleared.

docs.title: @ File References
docs.text:
In addition to persistent context, you can temporarily reference files using the @ symbol directly in your queries:

Syntax:

# Single file reference
@filename

# Multiple files
@file1.py @file2.py

# Paths with spaces (use quotes)
@"my document.txt"
@'path with spaces/file.md'

How it works:

  1. Type @ followed by a file path
  2. Press Tab for auto-completion and file browser
  3. Use arrow keys to select files
  4. The file content is automatically included in that message only
  5. References are replaced with filenames in the final message

Example:

# Quick file analysis
💬 > @README.md Summarize this project

# Compare files
💬 > @config.json @config.example.json What changed?

# Use with quotes for spaces
💬 > @"my notes.txt" Create a todo list from these notes

# Path completion
💬 > @src/ma[Tab]
# Shows: src/main.py, src/math.py, etc.

Differences from /add:

Feature /add @ reference Duration Entire session Single message only Storage Persistent context Temporary inclusion Best for Codebases you'll discuss repeatedly Quick one-time file checks Management Manual add/remove Automatic per message

docs.title: Configuration Guide
docs.text: YAICLI uses a layered configuration system to store your preferences and API keys. This guide explains all available configuration options and how to customize them.

docs.title: Configuration Hierarchy
docs.text:
YAICLI follows this priority order for configuration:

  1. Command-line arguments (highest priority)
  2. Environment variables
  3. Configuration file
  4. Default values (lowest priority)

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
YAICLI resolves its configuration directory in this order:

  1. YAI_CONFIG_DIR (explicit override)
  2. XDG_CONFIG_HOME/yaicli
  3. %APPDATA%/yaicli on Windows
  4. ~/.config/yaicli (fallback, e.g. Linux/macOS without XDG set)

The configuration file is config.ini inside that directory. It may contain an API key, so it is created with mode 0600 (and the directory with 0700). On a read-only HOME or container, YAICLI keeps working with defaults and only warns once when it cannot persist state.

The prompt history file follows XDG state conventions: $XDG_STATE_HOME/yaicli/history when XDG_STATE_HOME is set, otherwise ~/.yaicli_history.

docs.title: First-time Setup
docs.text:
1. Run a real model command once (e.g. ai "hi"); the default configuration file is created on first use
  2. Edit the file to add your API key and customize settings (or export YAI_API_KEY instead)

--version and --help never write state, so they are safe in read-only environments.

docs.title: Viewing Default Configuration
docs.text:
To view the default configuration template:

ai --template

docs.title: Configuration File Structure
docs.text:
The configuration file uses the INI format with the following sections:

[core]
PROVIDER=openai
BASE_URL=
API_KEY=
MODEL=gpt-5.2

DEFAULT_ROLE=DEFAULT
# auto detect shell and os (or specify manually, e.g., bash, zsh, powershell.exe)
SHELL_NAME=auto
OS_NAME=auto

# true: streaming response, false: non-streaming
STREAM=true

# LLM parameters
TEMPERATURE=0.3
FREQUENCY_PENALTY=0.0
TOP_P=1.0
MAX_TOKENS=1024
TIMEOUT=60
# JSON strings
EXTRA_HEADERS=
EXTRA_BODY=
REASONING_EFFORT=

# Interactive mode parameters
INTERACTIVE_ROUND=25

# UI/UX
CODE_THEME=monokai
# Max entries kept in history file
MAX_HISTORY=500
AUTO_SUGGEST=true
# Print reasoning content or not
SHOW_REASONING=true
# Text alignment (default, left, center, right, full)
JUSTIFY=default

# Chat history settings
CHAT_HISTORY_DIR=<tmpdir>/yaicli/chats
MAX_SAVED_CHATS=20

# Role settings
# Set to false to disable warnings about modified built-in roles
ROLE_MODIFY_WARNING=true

# Function settings
# Set to false to disable sending functions in API requests
ENABLE_FUNCTIONS=true
# Set to false to disable showing function output in the response
SHOW_FUNCTION_OUTPUT=true

# MCP settings
ENABLE_MCP=false
SHOW_MCP_OUTPUT=false

# Tool confirmation (set to false to restore silent execution)
TOOL_CONFIRM=true

# Maximum recursive tool-call rounds per request
MAX_TOOL_CALL_DEPTH=8

# Comma-separated API parameters to omit from requests, e.g. temperature,top_p
EXCLUDE_PARAMS=

# Agent context settings (v0.19)
# Max characters of one tool result kept in the context (0 = no truncation);
# the full output is saved to TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR.
TOOL_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS=32000
TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR=<chat-history-dir>/tool-outputs
# Token budget for one request; 0 derives 70% of the model context window.
CONTEXT_BUDGET_TOKENS=0

# Shell tool settings (v0.19)
# Max seconds a shell command may run (killed with its process group on timeout).
TOOL_TIMEOUT=120
# true = pass the full parent environment to shell commands (old behaviour);
# false = filtered environment, secrets such as YAI_API_KEY are not passed.
TOOL_ENV_INHERIT=false
# Shell commands may only run inside this directory (empty = current directory).
WORKSPACE_ROOT=

# Reliability settings (v0.19)
RETRY_ENABLED=true
RETRY_MAX=2
RETRY_BASE_DELAY=1.0
# Exit non-zero in one-shot mode when the tool-call depth limit is reached.
EXIT_ON_DEPTH_LIMIT=true

# Tool audit log (v0.19)
# Write one JSON line per tool decision to tool_audit.jsonl in the config dir.
TOOL_AUDIT=true

Comments in config.ini must be on their own line. Inline comments are not stripped by the INI parser and become part of the value (e.g. PROVIDER=openai # note would make the provider name invalid).

docs.title: Context Management
docs.text:
Conversation context is bounded on three levels; see Context & Limits for the full behaviour:

  • Per-tool truncation: TOOL_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS (default 32000 chars) keeps head/tail and spills the full output to TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR.
  • Token budget: CONTEXT_BUDGET_TOKENS (default 0 = 70% of the model window) is enforced before each request; over-budget history is trimmed by turn group, keeping assistant tool_calls and their tool results together.
  • REPL retention: INTERACTIVE_ROUND (default 25) is the number of chat turns kept in the REPL (×2 messages), not a token limit. MAX_HISTORY (default 500) only sizes the prompt history file (see Conversation & History).

Use /context to inspect the estimated usage and /compact [keep_rounds] to compact manually (see Command Reference).

docs.title: State Files
docs.text: Path Purpose <config-dir>/config.ini Main configuration (mode 0600) <config-dir>/roles/ Role definitions <config-dir>/functions/ User/exported function definitions <config-dir>/functions_manifest.json Version/hash manifest for stale copied-function detection <config-dir>/mcp.json MCP server configuration <config-dir>/tool_permissions.json Persistent tool allow rules (mode 0600) <config-dir>/tool_audit.jsonl Tool decision audit log <config-dir>/tool-outputs/ Spilled full tool outputs (unless TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR overrides) $XDG_STATE_HOME/yaicli/history or ~/.yaicli_history REPL prompt history CHAT_HISTORY_DIR (default <tempdir>/yaicli/chats) Saved chat sessions

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting Themes
docs.text:
YAICLI supports all Pygments syntax highlighting themes. Set your preferred theme with:

CODE_THEME = monokai

Browse available themes at: https://pygments.org/styles/

docs.title: Extra Headers and Body
docs.text:
You can add extra headers and body parameters to the API request:

EXTRA_HEADERS={"X-Extra-Header": "value"}
EXTRA_BODY={"extra_key": "extra_value"}

Example: Disable Qwen3's thinking behavior:

EXTRA_BODY={"enable_thinking": false}

Or limit thinking tokens:

EXTRA_BODY={"thinking_budget": 4096}

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Every option in the reference table above can be set with its YAI_* environment variable (these override the config file):

# Set API key via environment variable
export YAI_API_KEY="your-api-key"

# Use a different model
export YAI_MODEL="gpt-3.5-turbo"

# Disable streaming
export YAI_STREAM="false"

Environment variables take precedence over the configuration file settings.

Provider-specific keys that are not in the table (for example HF_PROVIDER, AZURE_ENDPOINT, AWS_*, AK/SK) are read by the individual provider implementations from the config file or their usual environment variables; they do not have a YAI_ alias.

docs.title: Provider-Specific Configuration
docs.text: See the Providers section for detailed configuration options for each supported LLM provider.

docs.title: Context & Limits
docs.text: Long agent tasks have a failure mode that chat tools do not: a single tool result (a log file, a directory listing, a web page) can be larger than the model's context window. YAICLI bounds this on three levels — per-tool truncation, a per-request token budget, and turn-group-aligned history trimming — and heals a context-length rejection instead of failing permanently.

docs.title: 1. Tool-output truncation
docs.text:
Every tool result is truncated before it enters the conversation:

  • only the head and tail of the output are kept, with a marker in the middle;
  • the full output is written to disk so nothing is lost;
  • the marker tells the model where the full text is and how to page through it.

The default cap is TOOL_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS=32000 characters (≈8k tokens). Built-in tools have per-tool caps on top of the global default:

Tool Approx. cap fs_read_file 64 KB fetch_webpage (body) 100 KB fs_search_files, fs_list_directory 48 KB execute_shell_command 32 KB web_search, MCP tools, default 32 KB

Full outputs are stored under TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR, which defaults to a tool-outputs/ directory under the chat-history directory. The truncated text includes the path so the model can read the rest:

{"file_paths": ["/path/to/tool-outputs/20261104-123456-execute_shell_command.txt"], "offset": 20000, "limit": 12000}

fs_read_file accepts two optional paging arguments (character based, applied per file):

Argument Meaning offset First character to return (0 = beginning of the file). limit Maximum number of characters to return (0 = read to the end).

The response keeps the usual path/success/content/size/error fields and adds offset/limit (the requested window), total_chars (full file length), returned_chars and truncated (whether content is only a window of the file). Paging works on the original file as well as on a spilled tool output; when reading a spilled output, remember it is the JSON text of the tool result, not the original file. fs_read_file results are themselves capped at 64 KB, so pass a limit comfortably below that (e.g. limit: 12000) to avoid the page being truncated again.

Notes:

  • Set TOOL_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS=0 to disable truncation (not recommended for agent loops).
  • The same truncation is applied to tool output printed in the terminal (SHOW_FUNCTION_OUTPUT), so a 1 MB shell result does not flood your screen.
  • If the spill file cannot be written (read-only disk, permission error), YAICLI degrades to plain truncation without the path — the request still succeeds.
  • Spilled files are created with mode 0600 on POSIX (file output may contain secrets); clean the TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR up periodically.

docs.title: 2. Token budget
docs.text:
Before each provider request, YAICLI estimates the tokens in the conversation (a stdlib heuristic: ~3.5 characters per token with corrections for CJK text, plus a fixed per-message overhead) and compares it with the budget:

Setting Meaning CONTEXT_BUDGET_TOKENS Token budget for one request. Default 0 = derive 70% of the model context window (fallback 128k tokens when the model is unknown). MAX_TOOL_CALL_DEPTH / --max-turns Bounds how many tool rounds one request may run (default 8).

If the conversation is over budget, YAICLI first trims mechanically — no extra API call, no extra cost — then sends the request. Trimming by message count alone is not enough: a tool_calls message must never be separated from its tool results, or every provider rejects the payload. YAICLI therefore trims by turn group:

  • a turn group is one user message plus the assistant/tool messages that follow it;
  • whole groups are dropped, oldest first;
  • an assistant message with tool_calls is always kept together with its tool results (zero orphan tool messages);
  • leading system/context messages are preserved;
  • one line is printed to stderr when trimming happens, so you know why old context disappeared.

docs.title: 3. Context-length self-healing
docs.text:
Even with estimation, a provider can reject a request with a context_length error (the exact window differs per model). When that happens, YAICLI:

  1. drops one more turn group (or trims further to the budget);
  2. retries the request once;
  3. if it still fails, prints an actionable error (provider, cause, suggestion) and exits with the usual error code — instead of the previous behaviour of failing every subsequent request.

In the REPL you can also recover manually with /clear or /compact.

docs.title: 4. Inspecting and compacting the conversation
docs.text:
In the interactive REPL:

Command Description /context or /ctx Show the estimated context usage: system prompt, history, tool output, remaining budget, and the budget being used. /compact [keep_rounds] Manually compact the conversation, keeping the last N turns (turn groups); older ones are dropped from the outgoing request. Without an argument the default retention applies. /clear Start over with an empty history.

Use /context when a session starts behaving as if it forgot earlier steps; then /compact to reclaim budget deliberately, or raise CONTEXT_BUDGET_TOKENS if your model has a larger window.

docs.title: 5. Session and memory limits
docs.text:
• INTERACTIVE_ROUND (default 25) is the number of chat turns kept in the REPL (×2 messages), not a token limit. Token trimming is described above.
  • MAX_HISTORY (default 500) is the number of entries in the prompt history file — it has no effect on the conversation context.
  • Tool outputs already spilled to TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR are not re-sent automatically; they only enter the context if the model reads them back.
  • Image input is bounded by the provider; keep images reasonably small (the local cache also holds the base64 payload in the session).

docs.title: Recommended settings for long tasks
docs.text:
[core]
# Leave at 0 to auto-derive 70% of the model window; set explicitly for small windows
CONTEXT_BUDGET_TOKENS=0
# Lower to reduce tokens per tool result if your model has a small window
TOOL_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS=16000
# More tool rounds before the depth limit stops the run
MAX_TOOL_CALL_DEPTH=12

docs.title: File Context Management
docs.text: YAICLI provides powerful file context management capabilities that allow you to include files and directories in your AI conversations. This helps the AI understand your codebase, configuration files, documentation, and any other relevant context.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
There are two ways to include files in your conversations:

  1. Persistent Context (/add): Add files/directories that stay in context for the entire session
  2. Temporary References (@): Reference files on-the-fly for a single message

docs.title: Persistent Context
docs.text: Use the /add command to add files or directories to your session context. These items remain available throughout your conversation until you remove them.

docs.title: Adding Files
docs.text:
# Add a single file
/add src/main.py
# Output: Added file to context: /path/to/src/main.py

# Add a directory (scans recursively)
/add tests/
# Output: Added directory to context: /path/to/tests/

# Add several files: /add takes one path per command
/add config.yaml
/add README.md

/add reads a single path per invocation (extra arguments are ignored); repeat the command for each file.

docs.title: Removing Context Items
docs.text:
# Remove by exact path
/context remove /path/to/src/main.py

# Remove by filename (partial match)
/context remove main.py

# Clear all context
/context clear

docs.title: Complete Command Reference
docs.text: Command Alias Description /add <path> - Add file/directory to context /context list /ctx list List all context items /context clear /ctx clear Remove all items /context add <path> - Same as /add /context remove <path> /ctx rm Remove specific item

docs.title: Temporary @ References
docs.text: For quick, one-time file inclusion, use the @ symbol directly in your messages.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
# Reference a single file
@README.md What is this project about?

# Reference multiple files
@src/main.py @config.yaml Explain the architecture

# The AI sees the file contents and responds based on them

docs.title: Paths with Spaces
docs.text:
Use quotes for filenames or paths containing spaces:

@"my document.txt" Summarize this

@'path with spaces/file.md' What does this do?

docs.title: Auto-completion
docs.text:
Type @ and press Tab to browse files:

💬 > @src/[Tab]
# Shows file browser:
# src/main.py
# src/utils.py
# src/config/

Use arrow keys to navigate and select files.

docs.title: File Reading Process
docs.text:
1. File Detection: YAICLI checks if the path exists
  2. Type Check: Determines if it's a file or directory
  3. Content Reading:
  4. Files: Read entire content
  5. Directories: Recursively scan (2 levels deep by default)
  6. Formatting: Content is formatted as Markdown code blocks
  7. Submission: Formatted content is sent to the AI as a system message

docs.title: Smart File Handling
docs.text:
Binary Files: Automatically skipped - Images: .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .ico - Archives: .zip, .tar, .gz - Compiled: .pyc, .pdf

Size Limits: Files larger than 1MB are skipped

Encoding: UTF-8 with error replacement for non-UTF-8 characters

docs.title: Directory Scanning
docs.text:
When you add a directory, YAICLI:

  1. Scans files recursively (default: 2 levels deep)
  2. Skips hidden files (starting with .)
  3. Ignores common patterns:
  4. .git/
  5. __pycache__/
  6. .venv/, venv/
  7. node_modules/
  8. .idea/, .vscode/
  9. .DS_Store

Example Directory Structure:

project/
├── src/
│   ├── main.py
│   └── utils/
│       ├── helpers.py
│       └── config.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_main.py
└── .git/          # Skipped
└── node_modules/  # Skipped

/add src/
# Includes:
# - src/main.py
# - src/utils/helpers.py
# - src/utils/config.py

docs.title: Codebase Analysis
docs.text:
# Add entire source directory
/add src/

💬 > Explain the architecture of this codebase
# AI now has full visibility into src/

docs.title: Configuration Review
docs.text:
# Multiple config files
/add .env
/add docker-compose.yml
/add config.yaml

💬 > Are there any security issues in this configuration?
# AI reviews all config files together

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
# Add error log and source file
/add error.log
/add src/handler.py

💬 > Why is this error happening in handler.py?
# AI correlates the error with source code

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
# Quick reference for documentation
@api-docs.md @docs/api-guide.md Implement this endpoint

# vs persistent context for long sessions
/add docs/

💬 > Help me implement user authentication
💬 > Now add password reset
💬 > Finally, add email verification
# docs/ stays in context for entire session

docs.title: When to Use /add (Persistent)
docs.text:
• Working on a specific feature: Add relevant source files
  • Code reviews: Include all files being reviewed
  • Debugging sessions: Keep error logs and source files available
  • Documentation: Reference docs while implementing features
  • Multi-step tasks: Avoid repeating file references

docs.title: When to Use @ (Temporary)
docs.text:
• Quick questions: One-time file checks
  • Comparing files: @file1.json @file2.json
  • Minimal context: Don't clutter the conversation
  • Ad-hoc analysis: Quick look at a file

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
1. Be Specific: Add only relevant files to avoid context bloat
  2. Clean Up: Remove items with /context remove when done
  3. Check Context: Use /context list to see what's active
  4. Use Quoted Paths: For files with spaces, use @"path"
  5. Combine Both: Use /add for core files, @ for temporary references

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
# Start a coding session
ai --chat

# Add core source files
/add src/
/add config.yaml

💬 > Add a new user registration endpoint

# Add a specific test file temporarily
@tests/test_auth.py Write tests for this

# Reference documentation once
@docs/api-spec.md Follow these specs

# Context still has src/ and config.yaml
💬 > Update the password validation

# Clean up when done
/context clear

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• File Size: Files > 1MB are skipped
  • Binary Files: Automatically filtered out
  • Directory Depth: Limited to 2 levels by default
  • Context Window: Total content limited by your model's context window
  • Session Scope: Context doesn't persist across different ai invocations

docs.title: File Not Found
docs.text:
💬 > /add nonexistent.py
Error: Path does not exist: /path/to/nonexistent.py

Solution: Use relative paths from current directory or absolute paths

docs.title: Image References
docs.text:
💬 > @diagram.png What does this show?

Expected behavior: image files (.jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif, .webp) referenced with @ are attached as image input for vision-capable providers; no "binary file" warning is produced. On providers without vision support the CLI warns that the image will be ignored.

docs.title: Binary File Warning
docs.text:
💬 > @document.pdf Summarize this
Warning: Cannot include @document.pdf: [Binary file omitted]

Expected behavior: non-image binary files (.pdf, .zip, compiled files, ...) are skipped; convert them to text (or use a different tool) first.

docs.title: Too Large Warning
docs.text:
💬 > @large-file.log
Warning: Cannot include @large-file.log: [File too large: 2097152 bytes - omitted]

Solution: Split the file or extract relevant portions

docs.title: Context Too Long
docs.text:
If the AI stops responding or behaves unexpectedly, the request may be over the token budget. YAICLI trims old conversation turns automatically and retries once when a provider rejects the request as too long; if it still fails it prints an actionable error.

Solution: 

/context            # show estimated token usage and remaining budget

docs.title: Headless & Scripting
docs.text:
YAICLI is designed to be scriptable: a one-shot run can be piped, redirected, parsed by jq, and its exit code can be trusted by CI. This page documents that contract.

The rule is simple:

  • stdout carries the result only (in text, json or stream-json form);
  • stderr carries everything else — labels, tool previews, warnings, errors, retry/trim notices;
  • the exit code describes the outcome.

docs.title: Quick examples
docs.text:
# One explicit one-shot run
ai -p "What is the capital of France?"

# Answer only, safe for shell substitution
summary=$(ai -q -p "Summarize README.md in one sentence")

# Machine-readable result
ai -p "List the files changed in the last commit" --output-format json | jq -r .content
# --json is a shorthand for --output-format json
ai -p "Summarize this repository" --json | jq -r .content

# Streaming events (one JSON object per line)
ai -p "Find and fix the failing test" --output-format stream-json | jq -c 'select(.type=="tool_call")'

# Pipe input into the agent
cat error.log | ai -p "Explain these errors and suggest a fix"

# CI: allow the shell tool for this run and fail the step when a tool is denied
ai -p "Run the test suite and summarize failures" \
  --allowed-tools "execute_shell_command" -y --fail-on-tool-denied

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Method Example Behaviour Prompt argument ai "explain this repo" One-shot with the given prompt Stdin echo hi \| ai Stdin content becomes the prompt Both cat app.py \| ai "review this" Stdin content is prepended to the prompt argument -p/--print ai -p "..." Explicit one-shot mode; never starts the REPL
  • When stdin is not a TTY, --chat is ignored (a warning is printed to stderr) because a REPL cannot read from a pipe.
  • -p/--print is the explicit form of a one-shot run. Use it in scripts for clarity: it forces the headless contract (plain output, no prompts/REPL) even on a terminal. --output-format other than text and -q also imply one-shot; --chat is then ignored with a stderr warning.
  • The REPL is only started by --chat (or by an interactive ai with no prompt).

docs.title: --output-format text (default)
docs.text: Human-readable text. In a non-TTY (pipe/redirect) this is plain text: no banner, no Rich Live animation, no ANSI/box drawing. The output ends with exactly one newline.

docs.title: --output-format json
docs.text:
One JSON object on stdout. All diagnostics go to stderr.

{
  "content": "The final assistant answer as markdown text.",
  "tool_calls": [
    {"name": "fs_read_file", "arguments": {"file_paths": ["README.md"]}, "result": "..."}
  ],
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 1234, "completion_tokens": 456},
  "model": "gpt-5.2",
  "provider": "openai",
  "error": null,
  "exit_code": 0
}
Field Meaning content Final assistant answer text tool_calls Ordered list of tool calls made during the run usage Token usage ({"prompt_tokens": ..., "completion_tokens": ...}). v0.19 reports zeros here because usage is not yet propagated from providers model, provider Effective model/provider for this run error Exactly null on success, otherwise {"kind": "<error kind>", "message": "<detail>"}. Possible kinds: auth, rate_limit, context_length, network, timeout, bad_request, provider, tool, config, depth_limit, interrupted, unknown exit_code Exit code the process will return (see below)

In v0.19 usage is intentionally reported as zeros — token usage from providers is not yet propagated to the payload (token accounting lands in a later v0.19 change). One limitation: failures that happen before a result exists (for example an invalid provider configuration, a missing API key during client creation, or a usage error such as exit 2) print a diagnostic to stderr and exit non-zero without emitting the JSON object; every run that reaches a result emits exactly one object. An interrupted one-shot run is reported both ways: exit 130 and, if JSON output was active, error.kind = "interrupted".

docs.title: --output-format stream-json
docs.text:
Newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON): one event object per line, in order. This is the format to use for progress UIs, cancellation and tool-trace collection.

Event When Fields turn_start A model request starts type, turn (0-based round index) text_delta The model streams answer text type, delta (new text since the previous chunk) tool_call The model requests a tool type, name, arguments (parsed JSON when possible) tool_result A tool has finished type, name, result (the tool result text as seen by the model, truncated as in context) usage Token usage is reported type, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens (zeros in v0.19) done The run finished type, exit_code, error (null or {kind, message})

Events are flushed per line. text_delta events stream during generation; tool_call / tool_result pairs are emitted at round boundaries (after the tools have executed), and usage / done are emitted at the end. Every event object has a type field; unknown event types must be ignored by consumers so that new event kinds can be added without breaking scripts. Example:

{"type": "turn_start", "turn": 0}
{"type": "text_delta", "delta": "I will check the "}
{"type": "tool_call", "name": "fs_read_file", "arguments": {"file_paths": ["README.md"]}}
{"type": "tool_result", "name": "fs_read_file", "result": "# YAICLI ..."}
{"type": "usage", "prompt_tokens": 0, "completion_tokens": 0}
{"type": "done", "exit_code": 0, "error": null}

docs.title: -q/--quiet
docs.text: Only the answer on stdout: no labels, no tool preview boxes, no progress. Errors still go to stderr. Combine with -p and either text or JSON output.

docs.title: Streaming and the terminal
docs.text:
Streaming stays on by default in a TTY. With a pipe or a redirect, YAICLI disables the Live region and cursor animation and prints the result plainly, so ai ... > file.md produces a clean file. Without -p, -q or a non-text output format, a TTY keeps the normal rich experience (labels and panels); the machine contract applies as soon as output is piped.

Use --no-stream if you want a single final block instead of streamed chunks.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success: an answer was produced (also informational commands such as --version / --list-*) 1 Handled failure: invalid config/provider, auth/API error, network failure, no input, unexpected error 2 Usage error: invalid option or argument (including an unknown --output-format value or an invalid --cwd) 3 A tool was denied and --fail-on-tool-denied was set 130 Interrupted by SIGINT (Ctrl+C) during a one-shot run or generation 141 Broken pipe (EPIPE): the producer side of a pipeline such as ai --help \| head -1. If the write wins the race, the same command may exit 0; it never exits 1 for a closed pipe.

Inside the interactive REPL, an error during one turn is printed and the session continues; leaving the REPL normally exits 0. Use one-shot (-p / prompt argument) when the exit code must reflect the request outcome.

docs.title: SIGINT (Ctrl+C)
docs.text:
• One-shot runs (including while the answer is generating): interrupts, prints one short line to stderr and exits 130 — no traceback.
  • REPL prompt: a single Ctrl+C clears the current input and stays in the REPL; pressing it a second time within ~2 seconds exits normally.
  • REPL generation: cancels the turn and returns to the prompt (a second Ctrl+C at the prompt exits).
  • Ctrl+D at the REPL prompt exits normally with 0.

docs.title: EPIPE (| head, closed pipes)
docs.text: Writing to a closed pipe never produces a traceback or a spurious non-zero error message: ai --help | head -1 is safe and exits 0/141. The same applies to long streamed answers piped into tools that stop reading early.

docs.title: Non-interactive approvals
docs.text:
In a pipe/CI there is no terminal to ask, so unapproved tool calls are denied by default. Three flags control this:

Flag Effect -y/--yes Auto-approve read-level tools only (read risk class). Write, network and exec tools are still denied unless separately allowed. With --shell in a non-TTY it is also the explicit switch that lets the generated command execute. --allowed-tools "a,b*" Per-run allowlist. Comma-separated tool names or glob patterns (fs_*, execute_shell_command). This is the explicit way to pre-approve write/exec tools. --fail-on-tool-denied Exit with code 3 if any tool call was denied (otherwise the model just receives the refusal and continues).

Persistent rules live in tool_permissions.json and are documented in Permissions & Safety. Danger-classified shell commands are always refused non-interactively, even when the tool itself is allowed.

TOOL_CONFIRM=false is still supported for fully unattended runs, but it grants every tool call without a prompt (apart from danger classification). Prefer --allowed-tools when you only need a few tools.

docs.title: Run limits
docs.text: Option Effect --max-turns N Maximum number of tool-call rounds for this run (N >= 1; maps to MAX_TOOL_CALL_DEPTH, default 8). When the limit is reached, the run stops with a depth_limit result; with EXIT_ON_DEPTH_LIMIT=true (default) a one-shot run exits non-zero. --cwd DIR Working directory for the run; also becomes the workspace root for shell tools. Paths outside the workspace are rejected. --output-format ..., -q, -p Output contract, described above.

docs.title: Non-interactive --shell
docs.text: --shell is an interactive convenience by default (it shows the generated command and asks before executing). When stdin/stdout is not a TTY, ai --shell "..." prints the generated command to stdout and does not execute it, exiting 0. Add -y/--yes to execute it in a trusted context; if the command itself then exits non-zero, the run exits 1.

docs.title: CI recipe
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# 1. The agent may read files and run the test command without prompting.
# 2. Any denied tool fails the job instead of silently degrading.
ai -p "Read the failing tests, find the root cause and write a short report to CI_REPORT.md" \
  --output-format json \
  --allowed-tools "fs_*,execute_shell_command" \
  --max-turns 12 \
  --cwd "$PWD" \
  --fail-on-tool-denied > result.json

jq -e '.exit_code == 0' result.json
jq -r '.content' result.json

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No output at all: errors go to stderr. Re-run and capture both: ai -p "..." >out.txt 2>err.txt.
  • jq: parse error: make sure you used -p/a prompt and --output-format json; text is the default. Warnings always go to stderr, so stdout remains parseable.
  • Tool denied in CI: add --allowed-tools for the tools the task needs; --yes alone only covers read-level tools.
  • Exit code 130 in CI: the job sent SIGINT (timeout/cancel) — check the CI timeout settings.
  • Long tasks stop early: raise --max-turns; the run reports a depth-limit message on stderr.

docs.title: Mode Switching (Chat / Execute)
docs.text: YAICLI offers multiple interaction modes to suit different needs. This page explains each mode and how to switch between them.

docs.title: Available Modes
docs.text: YAICLI has three primary interaction modes:

docs.title: 1. Chat Mode (💬)
docs.text:
Chat mode provides a natural conversation experience with the LLM, maintaining context and formatting responses with markdown.

Features: - Full conversation history and context tracking - Markdown and code formatting - Reasoning display for complex queries - Persistent chat storage and management

Best for: - Extended conversations - Complex questions requiring context - Learning and exploration

docs.title: 2. Execute Mode (🚀)
docs.text:
Execute mode specializes in generating and safely running shell commands based on natural language descriptions.

Features: - OS-specific command generation - Command review and editing before execution - Command output display - Safe execution with confirmation

Best for: - System administration tasks - File operations - Command discovery - Automating repetitive tasks

docs.title: 3. Quick Query Mode (Default)
docs.text:
The default non-interactive mode gives you quick answers without entering a persistent session.

Features: - Direct answers to questions - Support for piped input - Image input support via --image / -i - Fast responses with minimal overhead

Best for: - One-off questions - Quick information lookups - Image analysis with vision models - Script integration

docs.title: Command Line Switches
docs.text:
Use these flags when starting YAICLI:

# Start in chat mode
ai --chat "Optional chat title"

# Start in execute mode
ai --shell "Create a backup script"

# Quick query (default mode)
ai "What is the capital of France?"

# Quick query with image input
ai --image photo.jpg "What is in this image?"

docs.title: Interactive Mode Switching
docs.text: When in interactive mode (chat or execute), you can switch modes in several ways:

docs.text: Press the Shift+Tab key to toggle between Chat and Execute modes.

Type /mode followed by the mode name:

/mode chat   # Switch to chat mode
/mode exec   # Switch to execute mode

docs.text: The prompt changes to indicate your current mode: - Chat mode: 💬 > - Execute mode: 🚀 >

docs.title: Chat Mode Behavior
docs.text:
In chat mode: - The AI responds conversationally with rich formatting - Context is maintained between interactions - Input is treated as a conversation prompt

Example:

Assistant:

states simultaneously due to superposition...

docs.text:
In execute mode: - The AI interprets input as a request for a command - Generates appropriate commands for your OS and shell - Displays the command for review before execution

Example:

docs.title: Permissions & Safety
docs.text: An agent runs commands and writes files on your machine, so every tool call is gated. This page explains what YAICLI asks, how decisions are persisted, how to audit them, and how to run non-interactively without losing control.

docs.title: The default: confirm every tool call
docs.text:
TOOL_CONFIRM=true is the default. Before a tool runs, YAICLI shows a faithful preview of what will actually execute and asks:

╭─ Confirm tool call ────────────────────────╮
│ execute_shell_command                      │
│ risk: exec                                 │
│ command: du -sh .                          │
│ dangerous: no                              │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Execute tool? [y]once, [a]session, [A]always, [n]o:
Key Meaning y Allow this call only a Allow this tool for the rest of the session A Always allow — written to tool_permissions.json n Deny — the model receives a structured refusal and can adapt

Pressing Ctrl+C or sending EOF at the prompt is treated as a denial.

The preview shows the normalized arguments that will be executed, not the raw JSON from the model: JSON is repaired and validated first, shell commands are decoded and summarized with their risky flags, file edits show a diff excerpt, and file writes show the target path and whether the file will be created or overwritten. If the preview and the execution ever disagree, that is a bug.

docs.title: Risk levels
docs.text:
Every tool has a risk class. The class decides what --yes and rules may auto-approve.

Risk Built-in tools Notes read fs_get_filesystem_info, fs_list_directory, fs_read_file, fs_read_image, fs_search_files Read-only local access; the only class auto-approved by --yes write fs_write_file, fs_edit_file, fs_file_operations Change files on disk network fetch_webpage, web_search, get_weather Outbound requests exec execute_shell_command Runs arbitrary shell commands

MCP and custom tools default to exec because YAICLI cannot inspect what they do.

docs.title: Danger classification for shell commands
docs.text:
Shell commands are analysed with shlex (argv- and flag-based, not string matching) and can be flagged as dangerous: recursive/forced deletion, filesystem formatting, raw device writes, shutdown/reboot, recursive permission changes on /, find … -delete, piping a download straight into a shell, fork bombs, and similar. Safe commands such as git add, git status, ls -la are not flagged.

  • Interactively, a dangerous command needs an explicit confirmation even if the tool or a rule already allows execute_shell_command.
  • Non-interactively, a dangerous command is always denied, even with --yes or a matching rule.
  • With TOOL_CONFIRM=false there is no prompt to confirm with, so a dangerous command is denied as well.

Additional shell guardrails apply automatically: a timeout (TOOL_TIMEOUT, default 120 s), process group kill on timeout/interrupt, a filtered environment (YAI_API_KEY and other secrets are not passed to commands; restore the old behaviour with TOOL_ENV_INHERIT=true), and a bounded working directory (WORKSPACE_ROOT / --cwd).

docs.title: Persistent allowlist: tool_permissions.json
docs.text:
A (always allow) writes the permissions file in the config directory (~/.config/yaicli/tool_permissions.json by default). --allowed-tools is a per-run policy and is never written to it. The v2 format is:

{
  "version": 2,
  "always_allow": ["fs_read_file", "web_search"],
  "rules": [
    {"tool": "execute_shell_command", "argv_prefix": ["git", "status"]},
    {"tool": "execute_shell_command", "argv_prefix": ["pytest"]},
    {"tool": "fs_write_file", "path_glob": "src/**"}
  ]
}
Entry Meaning string in always_allow Allow that tool for every call (danger classification still applies) {"tool": ..., "argv_prefix": [...]} For shell commands: allow when the parsed argv starts with the given prefix {"tool": ..., "path_glob": ...} For file writes: allow when every path-like argument of the call (file_path, path, destination, ...) matches the glob (fnmatch-style, relative to the workspace)

The file is backward compatible: an old-style {"always_allow": ["execute_shell_command"]} keeps working. Rules are additive; a call is allowed when the tool is listed, or any rule for that tool matches the arguments. An argv_prefix rule only covers a single simple command (a pipeline, redirect or ;/&& chain still asks), and a path_glob rule only applies when every path argument of the call matches. A denied call returns a structured result to the model ({"error": "tool_denied", "reason": ...}) so it can choose another approach.

You can edit the file by hand; YAICLI reads it on the next run. The file is created with mode 0600 and lives next to the config file, which is created 0600 as well.

docs.title: Managing rules from the REPL
docs.text:
Command Description /permissions List session approvals, the persistent allowlist and the numbered rules /permissions revoke <tool-or-index> Remove a persistent permission (the tool then asks again)

The index is the rule number printed by /permissions; a tool name removes its always_allow entry, every rule for that tool, and its session approval. remove is accepted as an alias of revoke. Note that session approvals (a) are kept in memory and disappear when YAICLI exits; only A results persist.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
With TOOL_AUDIT=true (default), every tool decision is appended as one JSON line to tool_audit.jsonl in the config directory:

{"ts": "2026-11-04T12:34:56Z", "tool": "execute_shell_command", "risk": "exec", "decision": "denied", "source": "non_interactive", "args_summary": "du -sh .", "duration_ms": 0, "reason": "Dangerous shell command refused in a non-interactive session; ..."}
Field Meaning ts UTC timestamp tool Tool name risk Risk class of the tool decision allowed / denied / error source Why: prompt (you confirmed), session, persist, rule, allowlist (--allowed-tools), yes, disabled (TOOL_CONFIRM=false) or non_interactive args_summary Sanitized, truncated argument summary (shell commands are shown decoded; secrets such as API keys are redacted) duration_ms Tool execution time (0 for a denied call) reason Present for denials/errors: why the call was refused or failed

Set TOOL_AUDIT=false to disable, or point the log elsewhere by changing the config directory. The audit log records decisions, not full command output.

docs.title: Headless / non-interactive runs
docs.text:
When there is no TTY (piped stdin/stdout, CI), YAICLI cannot ask, so unapproved tools are denied by default. The flags that change this are:

Flag Effect --yes Auto-approve read-level tools only. With --shell in a non-interactive run it also means "execute the generated command" --allowed-tools "fs_*,execute_shell_command" Per-run allowlist by name or glob (* wildcards allowed), for this run only (not persisted) --fail-on-tool-denied Exit 3 when a tool was denied, instead of letting the model continue TOOL_CONFIRM=false Disable confirmation entirely; danger-classified shell commands are still refused

See Headless & Scripting for the full scripting contract.

Prefer narrow grants. Granting execute_shell_command does not make every command safe: individual commands are still danger-classified, but a non-malicious-looking command can still do damage. Rules with an argv_prefix are safer than a bare tool name.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• API keys: config.ini may contain API_KEY in plaintext. The file is created with mode 0600; prefer YAI_API_KEY (environment) on shared machines.
  • Workspace: shell tools run inside WORKSPACE_ROOT (or --cwd); a cwd outside it is rejected.
  • Environment: shell commands receive a filtered environment by default. TOOL_ENV_INHERIT=true restores the old behaviour — only do that if you trust every command the model may run.
  • Read-only / container environments: state writes are best-effort, so read-only commands such as --version and --help work without a writable HOME.
